title: Parliament of the United Kingdom
wiki_lead:
The Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is the supreme legislative body of the United Kingdom. It meets at the Palace of Westminster in London. It is bicameral, consisting of the House of Commons and the House of Lords, with the sovereign forming a third constitutional element. Acting together to legislate, these constitute the King-in-Parliament. Legislative authority has been devolved to the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Parliament, and Northern Ireland Assembly to differing degrees, while the UK Parliament retains authority to legislate in reserved matters and the power to legislate in devolved areas.
The House of Commons is the elected lower chamber, comprising 650 members elected from single-member constituencies using first-past-the-post voting. The House of Lords is the upper chamber and consists of the Lords Temporal, principally life peers, and the Lords Spiritual, bishops of the Church of England. The Commons has legislative primacy: under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the Lords can generally delay, rather than permanently block, legislation passed by the Commons. The government must retain the confidence of the House of Commons, and ministers are accountable to Parliament through debates, questions, and parliamentary committees.
The present Parliament was created on 1 January 1801 under the Acts of Union 1800, which created the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from the Parliament of Great Britain and the Parliament of Ireland. After the creation of the Irish Free State, the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927 changed its formal name to the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. During the 19th and 20th centuries, successive reforms expanded the electoral franchise, altered representation in the Commons, and reduced the powers of the Lords and the role of hereditary peers. The House of Lords also formerly exercised judicial functions, which were transferred to the newly created Supreme Court of the United Kingdom in 2009.
Legislation normally requires passage by both houses and royal assent, although the Parliament Acts allow certain bills to become law without the consent of the Lords. A Parliament may last for a maximum of five years, but may be dissolved earlier under the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022.

History

The Parliament of Great Britain was formed in 1707 following the ratification of the Treaty of Union by Acts of Union passed by the Parliament of England and the Parliament of Scotland, with both Acts of Union stating in article I that the kingdoms of England and Scotland would on 1 May 1707 "and for ever after, be united into one Kingdom by the name of Great-Britain", with article III stating that the kingdom will be represented by a single Parliament, to be named the Parliament of Great-Britain. grok_lead: The Parliament of the United Kingdom is the supreme legislative body of the country, comprising the House of Commons, the House of Lords, and the monarch, with core functions including the creation of laws, authorization of taxation and public spending, and scrutiny of the government's actions. It embodies parliamentary sovereignty as the highest legal authority, capable of enacting or repealing any law without override by courts or other institutions, a principle rooted in the unwritten constitution. Meeting at the Palace of Westminster in London since medieval times, Parliament has operated continuously for over nine centuries, evolving from advisory councils to the Anglo-Saxon kings into a bicameral legislature that asserts legislative primacy over the executive and judiciary. Key milestones include the Magna Carta of 1215, which first constrained monarchical authority through baronial demands for lawful governance, and the Bill of Rights 1689 following the Glorious Revolution, which affirmed Parliament's rights to free elections, speech, and petition while prohibiting royal suspension of laws. The House of Commons consists of 650 members elected by first-past-the-post from constituencies across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, typically for terms up to five years, while the House of Lords includes around 800 members mostly appointed as life peers for their expertise, alongside a reduced number of hereditary peers and bishops. This structure enables the Commons to initiate most legislation and control government formation via majority confidence, though the Lords provides revision and delay powers without veto over money bills. Defining characteristics include intense partisan debates, such as Prime Minister's Questions, and its role in devolution to regional assemblies since 1999, alongside ongoing tensions over Lords reform and electoral thresholds that have sparked controversies regarding democratic legitimacy and representation.
